opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something we've spent quite a bit of time trying to quantify. One way to frame it is to ask: if you want to reach a given level of performance, how much less compute do you need over time because of better algorithms? You can then compare that rate of "effective compute" gains from algorithms to the rate at which the physical compute used in training runs has been growing.

When we did this for language models, we found that the compute needed to reach a fixed level of performance has been halving roughly every eight months or so, though with pretty wide uncertainty. That's remarkably fast, faster than Moore's law. But the compute actually used in frontier training runs has been growing even faster, something like four to five times per year in recent years. So if you put those together, the picture is that compute scaling accounts for the larger share of performance improvements, maybe around two-thirds, with algorithmic progress accounting for the remaining third or so. In vision we found a broadly similar picture.

There are some important caveats. First, the two aren't really independent. Many algorithmic innovations, like the transformer, are valuable precisely because they scale well with more compute. Their benefit may be small at small scales and large at large scales, so it's somewhat artificial to separate them cleanly. Second, a lot of algorithmic progress is discovered through experimentation, which itself takes compute. So compute is an input into algorithmic progress too, and in that sense the importance of compute may be understated by a simple decomposition.

Third, these estimates focus on pretraining efficiency, measured as perplexity or something like it. They don't fully capture things like post-training improvements, better data, chain-of-thought prompting, tool use, and so on, which can give large gains in downstream capabilities at small cost. If you include those, algorithmic and data innovations look somewhat more important.

So my overall view is that compute scaling has been the dominant driver, but algorithmic progress is a substantial and complementary contributor, and the two reinforce each other. That has implications for forecasting: since compute is easier to measure and track than algorithmic insight, it gives us a reasonably good handle on where things are headed, and it also suggests that policy levers around compute are meaningful, even if they don't capture everything.

r001.rationale: The response says algorithmic gains reduced the compute needed for a fixed language-model performance level, while frontier training compute grew faster, and attributes roughly two-thirds of performance improvements to compute scaling. Its reference to pretraining efficiency measured by perplexity supports the next-word prediction target.

r002.rationale: It says the vision findings were “broadly similar,” which points back to a two-thirds compute, one-third algorithmic split, not roughly equal contributions.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe a recurring equal-contribution pattern in computer science outside AI.

r004.rationale: It notes that post-training and related changes can yield large gains at low cost, but does not say recent post-training algorithmic innovations contributed more than compute scaling on some tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So this is actually a question we've spent a lot of time on at Epoch, and I think the honest answer is that both matter a great deal, and they've been contributing roughly comparable amounts over the past decade or so.

Let me give you a sense of the numbers. On the compute side, the amount of compute used to train frontier models has been growing at something like four to five times per year since around 2010. That's an extraordinary rate, much faster than Moore's law, and it's been driven by labs spending more money, building bigger clusters, and running longer training runs, in addition to hardware getting better.

On the algorithmic side, we've tried to measure this by asking: how much less compute do you need today to reach a given level of performance than you needed a few years ago? When we look at language modeling, we find that the compute required to hit a fixed level of performance has been falling by roughly a factor of two or three every year. So algorithmic progress, if you express it in compute-equivalent terms, has been contributing something on the order of a doubling of effective compute every eight months or so. That's actually quite similar in magnitude to what you get from scaling physical compute.

So a reasonable first-pass answer is that it's been roughly a fifty-fifty split, with some uncertainty around that. I'd put the compute contribution as somewhat larger over the recent period, but not overwhelmingly so.

A couple of caveats, though. First, these two things aren't independent. A lot of what we call algorithmic progress is really progress in using compute more efficiently, and some innovations only become valuable once you have enough compute to exploit them. Transformers are a good example. They're not obviously better than older architectures at small scale, but they scale much better. So there's a sense in which algorithmic innovation is partly downstream of compute availability.

Second, algorithmic progress is harder to measure and much more uncertain. Compute you can count. Algorithmic gains you have to infer from performance trends, and there's a lot of noise, so I'd hold those estimates more loosely.

And third, looking forward, I think the question of which one dominates matters a lot for forecasting. Compute scaling is constrained by things like capital, energy, and chip manufacturing capacity, which we can forecast reasonably well. Algorithmic progress is constrained by the number of researchers and the ideas available, which is much harder to predict. If AI systems start contributing meaningfully to AI research itself, that could change the algorithmic side of the picture quite dramatically.

astra-6.text:
I think both are important, and it’s quite difficult to disentangle them. More compute lets you train larger models on more data, but algorithmic improvements can let you get the same performance with much less compute. So one useful way to compare them is to ask: how much additional compute would you need to match the benefit of a particular algorithmic improvement?

That gives you a common yardstick, although it’s imperfect. Some innovations enable capabilities that you wouldn’t readily get just by scaling an existing approach. And the two interact: having more compute makes it easier to run experiments and discover better algorithms, while better algorithms make larger training runs more productive.

So I’d be cautious about attributing progress entirely to either one. Compute scaling is a major driver and is relatively straightforward to measure. Algorithmic innovation is harder to measure, but that shouldn’t lead us to treat it as a minor contribution. If you’re forecasting future progress, you need to account for both, including how they reinforce each other.

sol-6.1.text:
I think both are very important, and it’s quite difficult to separate their contributions cleanly. More compute lets you train larger models on more data, but algorithmic improvements let you get more capability out of a given amount of compute.

One way to compare them is to ask: how much additional compute would you need, using an older algorithm, to match the performance of a newer one? That gives you a notion of algorithmic progress in compute-equivalent terms. On some tasks, those gains have been substantial, so I wouldn’t characterize progress as simply a story of throwing more compute at the same methods.

But the two also reinforce each other. More compute enables experiments that lead to better algorithms, and better algorithms make it worthwhile to invest in larger training runs. So their relative importance depends on the task and the period you’re looking at. Compute scaling is a comparatively predictable source of improvement; algorithmic innovation is harder to forecast, but it can substantially change what a given compute budget makes possible.
